newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British business says don't rule out EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British business says don't rule out EMU.

text.p: Fifteen top British business leaders weighed into the political row over future links with the European Union on Thursday, urging the government not to rule out participation in a single European currency.

In a letter to the Financial Times newspaper, they said a decision not to participate at this stage would be a gesture of "far from splendid isolation" that could be deeply damaging to Britain's interests.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke, the leading Europhile in a Conservative cabinet which is divided over European integration, hailed their comments as an endorsement of the government's strategy of deferring a decision until the currency is launched.
The letter said suggestions that Britain should rule out participation were based on a serious misunderstanding of monetary union and of Britain's interests as a trading nation.
"Many aspects of monetary union remain to be resolved. Leaving an empty chair at the table would mean that British interests would be unrepresented as crucial decisions were taken," it said.

Sir Bryan Nicholson, chairman of health care group BUPA and a former president of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), tacitly acknowledged that the letter had been a shot across the bows of right-wing "Eurosceptics" who have been pressuring the government to rule out joining EMU.
"There has been a tendency for those of us who trade in Europe to get on with our businesses and keep our head down," he said in a radio interview.

"We felt that it should be put above the parapet to let people know that there is a very strong body of opinion that is highly supportive of the opt-out and that doesn't see any need for the decision to be made today."
The Maastricht Treaty on European political and economic union gives Britain the right to opt out of a single currency, which is due to start up from 1999.

Prime Minister John Major has agreed to include a commitment in the Conservative election manifesto to hold a referendum on a single currency in the next parliament if a Conservative government decides to join. An election is due by May 1997.
But Major has resisted pressure from Eurosceptics to rule out membership, saying he would decide when monetary union starts whether it is in Britain's interest to participate.
Nicholson said it was still not clear whether it would ultimately be in Britain's interest to join.
"We shouldn't make a decision now which we don't need to make now, but we should influence the way that decision is made in the best British national interest," he said.

Clarke said he fully supported the views expressed in the letter, whose signatories included the chairman or chief executive of firms such as B.A.T Industries, British Aerospace, British Petroleum, Glaxo Wellcome and Unilever.
"It's absolutely key that we remain involved negotiating on these matters," Clarke told reporters.

"British interests are heavily involved, whether we go into the single currency or not. As we are the best performing major economy in western Europe, our influence is absolutely crucial to make sure Europe is the kind of Europe we want."
Britain's Euro-sceptics are determined to prevent the country joining a single currency because they believe it would mean an irrevocable loss of national sovereignty.

But many industrialists whose main markets are in Europe fear non-participation could mean their exclusion from the free-trading benefits of the EU's single market, while some bankers believe the City of London could lose its role as the world's leading financial centre.
